title: The Prophets and Apostles Call the Spirit God’s Own
english: … him, and that he alone knows the things of God and comes upon all, they say such things as these.

Moses in Genesis, speaking in the person of God: “My spirit shall not remain in these men for ever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3). Haggai likewise, with the divine voice: “I am with you, and my spirit stands in your midst” (Haggai 2:4-5). Zechariah likewise: “But hear my words, and receive my statutes, which I command by my spirit to my servants the prophets” (Zechariah 1:6).

Isaiah, speaking from the Father to the Son: “My spirit, which is upon you, and the words which I have put in your mouth, shall not fail from your mouth or from the mouth of your seed” (Isaiah 59:21). By his seed he means the faithful, whom he also called to adoption as sons. And again, in the person of the Son: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Isaiah 61:1). That these things were brought to fulfilment in the economy of salvation Matthew stated thus: “So that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which says: Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased; I will put my spirit upon him” (Matthew 12:17-18). And again, in the person of the Father: “For a spirit shall go forth from me” (Isaiah 57:16 LXX).

And in Ezekiel the Most High Father calls our spirit “your” spirit, but names the Holy Spirit his own, since it proceeded from him by nature: “And I will give you a new heart and a new spirit; and I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh; and I will put my spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26-27). And in Joel: “I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28).

And that these things have been accomplished Paul wrote to Titus: “When our saving grace appeared, not by works that we ourselves had done, but according to his great mercy, he gave us new birth through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ” (Titus 3:4-6).

And when did he pour him out? When Christ breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). “Poured out” is well said, too, since the Spirit proceeded from him consubstantially, like water, and is a divine ointment, as we will show at the right time in the places that suit it. And so is “upon all flesh”. For these words fit the essence of the Holy Trinity, which is shared by many together, and not a created rational nature, which cannot be shared. For nowhere was it written, nor would it be plausible to say, “I will pour out of the archangel”; but “of my spirit”, and not even that without qualification, but “upon all flesh”.

And David, too, cries out in supplication: “Do not take your holy spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11); and again: “Your holy spirit will guide me on level ground” (Psalm 143:10). And Matthew, quoting the Son: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20); that is, not you, who are created, but the uncreated Spirit of God.

Paul, too, writes to the Corinthians in his first letter: “What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him, God has revealed to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God, except the Spirit of God. Now we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things freely given us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:9-12).

He spoke of the good things “prepared” by God, and said that “the Spirit” “revealed” them, as one who gives together with God; and he said “his Spirit” in contrast to our spirit. And taking care once more that the Spirit should not be thought an angel or some other created spirit, he added: “We have not received the spirit of the world”, that is, one that came into being, “but the Spirit who is from God”, that is, by elimination, the one who proceeded from the hypostasis of God. And he showed that the Spirit alone knows the things of God, as Lord, and as being the same in nature with the Father. For “the servant”, as he says in the Gospel, “does not know what his master is doing” (John 15:15).
But he did not go on to say, as he did of man, “that dwells in God”, lest the God who is not composite be thought composite.

To the Ephesians: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30). To the Romans: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you; but if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). To the Galatians: “And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father” (Galatians 4:6). To the Philippians: “For I know that …” (Philippians 1:19)

title: The Spirit of God, Uncreated and Proceeding from the Father
english: … this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:19).

Observe, then, how merely calling him “Spirit of God”, and adding “my” and “your”, has also signified this plainly: that he is uncreated and God, and that he holds the name not as something brought in from outside, but because by nature he is the very thing he is called.

And that he is written “Spirit of the Son” likewise showed his fellowship of nature with the Son, so that he should not be thought the Son’s creature. For how could the Son have created for his own Father, as though the Father did not have it from himself before, that which both is and is written “Spirit of God”? That is not only blasphemous but foolish as well. “Spirit of Christ” may be understood as “power of Christ”, in the way it is said: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). For since these blessed hypostases came forth from the nature of one Father, and not by a creative act, they are traced back to the same One.

For so that no one may suspect that he has a beginning or an end, but may truly believe, from the procession that belongs to his nature, that he is the Spirit of God, breathed forth without beginning and not made like one of the other ministering spirits, the Lord teaches in the Gospel according to John and says: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). He did not say “is created”. For every begetting and every procession is brought about through what is equal and alike; and most of all, beyond every other, is the begetting and procession from the one Father, in the unity of his own Godhead. But among creatures the original goes before in time; with God it is not so: they subsist together and have come forth together.

In harmony with the Lord, John too proclaimed that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and does not differ from him. He shows that the Spirit, a partial grace of the Father, embraces, so to speak, the whole of God the Father, who cannot be circumscribed, and is found among the faithful as a partial grace, when he says: “For by this we know that we abide in him and he in us, by his Spirit, whom he has given us” (1 John 4:13). In the same way the Son said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); and: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28).

For nothing at all that falls short in essence, or in time, or in glory, can display the whole truth, or be of the same kind and have equal knowledge; nor could anyone gain a share in true Godhead through a creature. The Holy Spirit is given, not by cutting him into portions, but on the principle of participation, and so that he may not be thought to dwell in us as one different from the Father in nature or in will.

At the same time “the son of thunder” (Mark 3:17) showed that where the Holy Spirit is, God the Father is present, whose Spirit he is. God himself proclaimed this beforehand when he said: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16). So again the opposite makes plain that whoever does not have the Spirit of God as true God does not have the Father either; and where he is not, there is nothing true, nothing safe, nothing firm.

So, conversely, anyone at all who speaks of him, even if he happens to be a heretic, if asked what spirit he is talking about, says, “The Holy Spirit”; and if the question is put to him again, “Which Holy Spirit?”, he must say, to make it as plain as possible, “The Spirit of God”, since the other spirits are not his in essence.

But the heretics, a trouble to themselves and to their hearers, slander with violent arguments the saints who are better than both us and them, who far surpass us, and who uttered oracles about the Holy Spirit; and no one may lay down rules against them. For they say, word for word: “When God says, ‘My servant Isaiah’ (Isaiah 20:3), and ‘Israel my firstborn son’ (Exodus 4:22), does the syllable ‘my’ show that human nature has something in common with the nature of God? Just as he said this, then,” he says, “as the cause of their being, so too he called the life of their souls ‘my spirit’.”

If they had any regard for truth and precision, they would not have stumbled so badly. For first, by the very names “Isaiah” and “Israel” he showed that they were men; and he added the “my” to them as a special honour, as men who belonged to him by their deeds. He called Isaiah “servant”, that is, a member of his household, and Israel “firstborn”, as the first to begin to worship him, and as standing in the rank of a son through God’s favour and care toward him. title: “My Spirit”: Kinship of Nature and the Spirit’s Divine Names
english: … true Son and the true Spirit, when God says it, shows that they are akin to him in nature; but of all the others it shows that they belong to him by lordship or by faith. So we too are used to saying, of those who share our essence, “my son, my spirit”, but of other things, “my field, my horse”, and also “my God”.

For in the same way, it is not his being called simply and without qualification Son, and Only-begotten, and Word of God, and Christ, that shows that the Word of the divine nature, who subsists in his own right, was begotten from the hypostasis of God; it is his having the syllable “my” or “your” joined to these names. So when God says, “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17), and again, “My good word” (Psalm 45:1), and, “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm 132:17), we in turn acclaim him: “Your Son, your Only-begotten, your Christ.”

Nor, indeed, does the fact that Scripture writes of us with the same or a like name, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:2), drag the Son of God away from the Godhead by the sharing of a name. So with the Holy Spirit: it is not his being called simply “spirit”, but the joining to the name of “my”, as from God, or of “your”, as from creation, or of the word “holy” or “incorruptible” or “everlasting”, that shows that he has proceeded from the Father’s hypostasis. Nor, indeed, does the fact that the ministering spirits and our own spirits are called by the same name, “holy” or “everlasting”, drag him away from being by nature the true Spirit of God.

For even in the riddles that speak of him there is always some declaration of his divine nature and power. But created things received holiness and everlastingness in the measure of their own nature, and do not possess these things by nature of themselves at all.

Otherwise, are these heretics not found accusing themselves, since they readily accept the “my” said of the Son of God, and the “holy” and the “everlasting”, as announcing that he has the same divine nature? Then, besides this, in the proofs set out above it was not the life of our souls that he named “spirit”, but his own Holy Spirit. For when we already had our own spirit, the Spirit of God was given us as well. The Father said, “My spirit shall not remain in these men” (Genesis 6:3), and the Son, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). And it is clear that it was to those who already had our own spirit that these words about the divine Spirit were spoken.

As the Son, then, the Word of God, is begotten as a son, so the Holy Spirit proceeds as spirit, and not by way of creation. And as there is no variation of essence, power or glory between the only-begotten Son and God the Father, but every difference, if it is right to say so, between him and creation, so it is with the one divine Spirit as well.
So it is more just not even to listen to what heretics say than to listen to it, even without accepting it.
That the divine nature of the Holy Spirit is shown by various names.

As we said at the beginning, the oracles bear witness, in the second place, that the Spirit of God has various names fit for God. To the propositions before us these names bring much further, exalted meaning, and a relation that is above all things, bound closely to the Father and the Son, and beyond the most fitting expression. They unfold, some of them, his divine nature, and others his sovereign power. They console our weakness in reaching him worthily, whether in the expression of words or in the contemplation of the mind. And they give us boldness to call him, without danger, consubstantial with God, and to trust in his sanctification.
We do not find any of the other spirits deemed worthy to be called by these names; and that which alone and by nature is all these things is no one among all things, but God.

These are the names. Holy Spirit, as is written everywhere. Spirit of holiness, and sanctifying, as Paul writes to the Romans: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was declared Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness” (Romans 1:1-4). And again: “That the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:16). And elsewhere: “But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits for salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13).
